default.p.n2dokkai-mock-q1.vietnamese:
I think hardly anyone associates the word "regret" with anything good. I used to feel the same way. If only I had listened properly at the time; why did I laugh awkwardly to gloss over something important; if only I had looked at things a little more positively... The list of such thoughts would never end.

However, recently I have begun to think that having many regrets is not necessarily a bad thing. A life filled with regret is proof of how often we have faced situations and made choices for ourselves. Regret over things we did not choose for ourselves will surely lead to the determination: "Next time I make a decision, it must be my own choice." I want to turn regret into a stepping stone toward becoming a better version of myself.

Leo Ieiri - Asahi Shimbun, April 10, 2018
*1 Kiri ga nai: Having no end. Here, it means there are many.
*2 Akashi: Evidence, proof.

default.p.n2dokkai-mock-q12.vietnamese:
The most distinctive characteristic of animals is their ability to move. So what is the relationship between activities such as running, flying, and swimming and body size?

The first thing that is easy to notice is that the larger a creature is, the faster it tends to be. From ants to mice, mice to cats, and cats to dogs, as body size increases, so does running speed. Looking at the personal best records of land-running animals, larger animals are generally faster. The same is also true of flying and swimming animals. High speed provides a major advantage in hunting prey and escaping predators, so it is an advantage of having a large body.

However, if we assume that speed will continue increasing without limit as body size grows, reality is not so simple. The fastest land animal is said to be the cheetah, which can reach 110 km/h. A cheetah weighs about 55 kg, and in reality, even if its weight increases further, its speed hardly increases. Once its weight exceeds 100 kg, its running speed actually decreases. A similar decline in speed as animals approach the upper limit of body size can also be seen among swimmers; tuna (80 kg) boast speeds of 100 km/h, whereas whales swim much more slowly. Once animals become as enormous as elephants or whales, they no longer need to worry about being attacked by predators, so perhaps they only need to leisurely graze or calmly scoop up krill.

By Tatsuo Motokawa, from "Elephant Time, Mouse Time," published by Chuokoron-Shinsha.
※1 Cheetah: a cheetah　※2 Whale: a whale　※3 Predator: a creature that catches and eats other creatures　※4 Krill: krill

default.p.n2dokkai-mock-q17.vietnamese:
When we judge things and situations, a factor called subjectivity becomes involved. Even people who always say, “Compared with other people, I view everything objectively,” cannot make objective judgments like a computer.

While a computer processes information in a “bottom-up” manner—making judgments based on the data it collects—human beings operate in a “top-down” manner, judging situations through “subjectivity” combined with the knowledge, beliefs, and emotions they have formed throughout their lives.

There was an experiment investigating how strongly human thinking is top-down. It went as follows:

There were thumbtacks in a box, with a candle and a lighter beside it. Participants were told: “Use all these materials to make the candle stand upright and light it. However, you may not place the candle directly on the floor or table.” What would you do?

The correct answer is to “use the thumbtacks to attach the box containing them to the wall, then place the candle in it.” However, when participants actually attempted this problem, even students at prestigious universities had a success rate of only about 10%. Although they could see the “box containing the thumbtacks,” they were trapped by top-down processing—the inference that the box was “something for holding thumbtacks”—and could not think of using the box itself as a “candle holder.”

Even when observing something new for the first time, the top-down thinking that characterizes human beings naturally reveals itself.

With our perception distorted by subjective preconceptions, we cannot see other people accurately. The stronger our top-down thinking, the more likely we are to overlook other people’s potential or weaknesses.

Nevertheless, removing knowledge, emotions, or beliefs from human beings is extremely difficult. If so, then, on the basis of recognizing that “human beings are very prone to top-down thinking,” making an effort to view matters objectively, even if only slightly, becomes an extremely important key to seeing through other people.

Rie Ueki, excerpted from “The Brain Lies Naturally,” Kadokawa Shoten.

default.p.n2dokkai-mock-q2.vietnamese:
The following passage was written by a top professional shogi player.

When shogi players are young, they usually compete by making full use of their calculating ability, memory, and quick reflexes. As they grow older, however, it is normal for them to gradually shift toward intuition and a broad perspective.

I believe that intuition and a broad perspective are used by comparing a position with one’s own accumulated rules of experience, even within the brief interval of less than a second. Therefore, they cannot be used without having accumulated a certain level of practical experience. In other words, successful and unsuccessful experiences are transformed into nourishment for personal growth, and that is a precious asset.

（Middle section omitted）

Even though intuition is a choice—whether to keep or discard something—made in a brief moment of less than a second, it is still something for which we can clearly explain why we chose that move. It is not an arbitrary or blindly thoughtless choice; ultimately, it arises from everything we have built up through our experiences.

Yoshiharu Habu, 『The Power of Intuition』, PHP Institute Publishing
※1 Shogi player: a professional player of shogi　※2 Game: a shogi match　※3 Broad perspective: a view of the whole position
※4 Selection: choosing what to absorb and what to discard　※5 Blindly: without thinking

This notice is posted at Yamanaka City Hall.

【We kindly ask for your cooperation】
The national government has requested that water and electricity be conserved this summer. Accordingly, our city hall has decided on the following measures, and we kindly ask everyone for their cooperation.

・Set air conditioners to 28°C.
・From June through September, wear light, comfortable clothing. Do not wear jackets or neckties.
・During the lunch break (12:00–1:00), turn off half of the lights in the building.
・During the lunch break and after the office closes (from 5:00 p.m. onward), operate only 2 of the 4 elevators.
・As a general rule, if you are going only one or two floors, try to use the stairs as much as possible.
・Wednesday is designated as No Overtime Day; try to leave work before 5:30 p.m.

Yamanaka City Mayor　Ichiro Suzuki

When was marketing introduced to Japan? When I ask students this during lectures, the results are very interesting. For the moment, I ask them to guess roughly when it was after the war, but what do you think the results will be? First, when do you yourself think it was?

The reactions were roughly as follows: the 1960s accounted for 10%, the 1970s for 40%, the 1980s also for 40%, and the 1990s for 10%. In other words, the common image seems to be that it began sometime in the 1970s and continued into the 1980s.

So when was the correct answer? There are records documenting this. The answer is 1955.

Naoto Yamamoto, from "Whose Fault Is It When Products Don't Sell? An Introduction to Misunderstandings about Marketing," Shincho Shinsho.

default.p.n2dokkai-mock-q6.vietnamese:
eSports is short for Electronic Sports. It refers to treating competitive computer games (video games) as a sport. Overseas, there are professional players and professional tournaments, and the number of eSports players worldwide is said to have exceeded 100 million. On the other hand, some argue that eSports cannot be recognized as a sport. Perhaps this is because sport has traditionally been associated with physical activity in nature, whereas eSports does not present such a healthy image.

Ultimately, what is sport? In prehistoric times, before writing was used, people hunted and gathered food. Although these activities were means of survival, recreational activities also existed during their free time. Paintings of horseback riding and wrestling have been discovered on rock walls. People may also have thrown spears. These can be regarded as sports that used familiar animals and tools around them.

Ancient Greece is famous as the place where the Olympics were first held, and during that period many different competitions were organized and systematically standardized. There also seem to have been competitions involving balls and competitions that made use of the most advanced chariots of the time. In medieval Europe, competitions using guns once employed in warfare also became a form of sport, in addition to these activities. In the modern era, when the Industrial Revolution took place, workers enjoyed sports as a way to relieve stress after being freed from long hours of labor. The same is true today: many people probably play sports after a long workday. At such times, people use familiar tools as well as the most advanced tools available. That tool is the computer.

Viewed in this way, should eSports not be fully recognized as a sport?

default.p.n2dokkai-mock-q9.vietnamese:
When I was providing mental-health counseling at a certain workplace, the movement patterns of the employees became a topic of discussion. Because it was a workplace with a large floor area, the movement paths had been designed to make employees' movements efficient, but this apparently was not popular with the employees.

If movement paths are improved skillfully, unnecessary movements can be eliminated. Fewer movements mean less physical fatigue, and people will probably be able to concentrate more on their work. With this in mind, they changed the arrangement of the departments, but the employees gradually began to feel that they had lost their psychological breathing room.

Previously, while moving around the workplace, people would occasionally run into unexpected colleagues, senior coworkers, or junior coworkers and chat enthusiastically for a while. They were not necessarily discussing any particular issue; sometimes new ideas emerged from such casual conversations. Even when no ideas emerged, their moods relaxed somewhat, and they found the motivation to begin their next task.

As I wrote last week, when stress continues for a long time, we lose our inner sense of ease. When facing a problem, we can think in only one direction. We cannot consider possibilities from multiple perspectives, and problems that could otherwise have been overcome become impossible to solve.

At times like these, simply engaging in small talk and entering a completely different state of mind can give us fresh perspectives.

Recently, as computers have become widespread, the number of workplaces where communication is handled only by email has also increased. [On the one hand], this eliminates unnecessary conversations (A), [but on the other hand], it also [reduces/erases] the flexible handling of problems and the emergence of new ideas (B).

Oono Yutaka, June 19, 2016, Nihon Keizai Shimbun

default.p.n2dokkai-p100.outline.0.label: Refuting the belief that cigarettes reduce stress
default.p.n2dokkai-p100.outline.0.note: Cigarettes do not relieve stress; they only temporarily eliminate the symptoms of nicotine craving.

default.p.n2dokkai-p100.outline.3.label: Benefits of quitting smoking
default.p.n2dokkai-p100.outline.3.note: Quitting smoking truly relieves stress, improves mental health, and strengthens social relationships.
default.p.n2dokkai-p100.outline.4.label: Advice and confidence in successfully quitting smoking
default.p.n2dokkai-p100.outline.4.note: Emphasizes the damage tobacco causes to people’s lives and asserts that quitting smoking is entirely possible.
default.p.n2dokkai-p100.vietnamese:
To state the conclusion briefly, cigarettes do not relieve stress at all. The feeling that "my stress has decreased" after smoking is actually the illusion that the disappearance of nicotine-withdrawal symptoms—such as irritability, difficulty concentrating, and restlessness—when nicotine enters the body constitutes stress relief.

What did your first cigarette taste like? In most cases, you probably felt uncomfortable rather than pleasant. This is because nicotine does not improve one's mood, even when it enters the body. This is completely different from alcohol, which can make people feel intoxicated the first time they drink it.

If you continue smoking, the brain becomes sluggish and dopamine, a brain hormone related to feelings of happiness, becomes harder to release. When the nicotine in the body runs out, withdrawal symptoms gradually reduce feelings of happiness in all areas of life, including eating and working. Under these circumstances, smoking to replenish the nicotine that has fallen in the body is when you finally feel satisfied.

By comparison, it is like wearing a pair of tight shoes continuously and then feeling relieved when you take them off. You could not say that "tight shoes relieve stress in your feet."

Conversely, if you quit smoking, everyday stressors such as the nicotine-withdrawal symptoms caused by cigarettes disappear, and your mental well-being improves. At smoking-cessation clinics, it is often reported that problems in interpersonal relationships decrease and that people become more considerate toward pedestrians and other drivers when driving a car.

Since it is known that half of all smokers die prematurely from smoking-related diseases, quitting is healthier than continuing, even if it requires considerable effort. Even if we generously concede that cigarettes can relieve stress, if smoking damages your health, that is putting the cart before the horse. Nicotine-withdrawal symptoms last for at most about 1 week. Quitting smoking is certainly possible.

default.p.n2dokkai-p101-g1.vietnamese: In Japan, people use chopsticks when eating. During a meal, the chopsticks are placed horizontally, nearest to the diner. I used to think this was only natural. However, in China and Korea—places where chopsticks are also used at meals—the custom is different: the chopsticks are placed vertically on the diner's right, with the ends that go into the mouth pointing toward the person sitting opposite. Why are chopsticks placed horizontally in Japan? There are said to be two reasons. Chopsticks are thin and somewhat dangerous objects, so pointing their ends at another person is considered rude. In addition, in Japan, food is traditionally regarded as something received from nature and the gods. The area in front of the horizontally placed chopsticks represents the human world, while the other side represents the world of the gods. The chopsticks are precisely what separate the world of the gods from the human world.

default.p.n2dokkai-p102.vietnamese:
I think the one thing you absolutely should do in your twenties is "experience the biggest failure of your life".

Failure later in life takes a long time to recover from, economically, socially, and emotionally. However, if it happens in your twenties, you can recover from almost anything. So don't be afraid to take risks; challenge yourself with whatever you can.

When I ask successful people about their experiences, most of them have experienced major failures in their teens or twenties. I often hear stories of failures so frightening that I feel I might faint just listening to them—failures I would never want to experience myself.

And yet, strangely enough, those very people recount these stories with great delight.

Rather than regretting their failures, they even seem somewhat proud, as if to say, "How on earth did I dare to do something so bold? But I have to admit, I was pretty amazing."

For example, borrowing 100 million yen and suddenly going into business... From an ordinary perspective, I see this as nothing more than reckless, blind risk-taking. But when I hear the story, I am overwhelmed by the sheer scale of that recklessness.

If you experience a major failure while you are young, everything that happens afterward will become a positive asset. Conversely, if you always choose the safe path and avoid failure from the outset, you may gain a life without failure—but in exchange, you will have a life without any drama.

Taking risks and experiencing failure are the most valuable assets a person can build in their twenties.

To achieve "remarkable accomplishments that make others marvel" in the future, it is important not to fear "terrible failures so awful that you have to cover your eyes and cannot bear to look at them."

default.p.n2dokkai-p104.vietnamese:
The second thing you should do while in your twenties is "find something you truly love."

However, what I really want to say is: "Precisely because you are in your twenties, do the things you like."

Then, after some time has passed, people may reach a state in which they can no longer feel or think deeply about anything. Don't you also know people in their thirties who are like that?

Some people may think that once they become adults, they cannot keep doing what they like, and that patiently completing things they dislike is instead proof that they have entered their twenties and moved beyond their teenage years.

The reason is that when they reach their thirties, many people begin to wonder, "Is it really okay to continue like this?" Although they constantly think, "I want to do something that bears more of my own distinctive mark," the pressure and stress of everyday life gradually numb their emotions.

Of course, it is entirely possible that what you love will change after several years. However, since the "prototype of talent" is essentially the same, the earlier you begin, the better.

default.p.n2dokkai-p105.vietnamese:
Regarding the word "company" (kaisha), I had a bitter experience. It happened nearly 20 years ago, when I gave a lecture on Japan's corporate capitalism at a university in China.

I said, "Your China is socialist," and wrote "socialism" on the blackboard. Then I explained, "In contrast, Japan is corporate capitalism," by reversing the order of the kanji in "society" (shakai) and "company" (kaisha). Since I did not know Chinese, a Chinese person who knew Japanese interpreted what I said. However, even after the interpreter had translated and repeated my words, the students listening showed absolutely no reaction. I had thought I had just told a witty story, but I ended up feeling disappointed.

Looking back, their reaction was only natural. China has a word for "society," but it does not have the word "company" (formed by reversing those characters), so even if I said, "Socialism and corporate capitalism are opposites," they could not understand what I meant.

default.p.n2dokkai-p106.outline.0.note: A plan does not have to be something grand at work; it can also be a small, familiar intention in everyday life.

default.p.n2dokkai-p106.outline.1.note: Opportunities to make plans are everywhere; recognizing and using free time instead of being lazy can make life more interesting.
default.p.n2dokkai-p106.outline.2.label: How the author makes use of unexpected free time

default.p.n2dokkai-p106.outline.3.label: The value of encountering differences and having new experiences
default.p.n2dokkai-p106.outline.3.note: Doing something new creates the “friction” of innovation and adds flavor to life; even disappointment may prove useful later.
default.p.n2dokkai-p106.vietnamese:
When people hear the word “planning,” they probably think of something connected with work or something grand and ambitious. However, to give a more familiar example, thinking, “Next Sunday is a rare day off, so let’s do something,” is also planning. Thinking, “I finished work an hour earlier than usual. I normally take the train home, but maybe I’ll try taking several buses instead and do this along the way,” is also planning.

There are many opportunities in daily life to think about and carry out plans. I think how interesting your life is changes greatly depending on whether you notice them. If you simply lie around watching television or reading manga just because you get home early, that is a real “waste.” By using that hour to make an interesting plan, life becomes much more interesting.

If it were me, and a scheduled task suddenly disappeared from my calendar, leaving me with an unexpected free hour, I would use the time to do something I would normally never do. Instead of thinking, “I have an extra hour, so I’ll take care of that thing I’ve always thought I should do,” I would think of it as an hour suddenly given to me as a gift from God and try doing something I almost never do.

For example, climbing to the top of a tall building, looking out over the surroundings, finding a spot that seems interesting, and then going there can be surprisingly enjoyable.

There are also parks that we always pass by but have never entered. Try walking into one of those parks and sitting on the swing. Then, the next time you pass that park, you will know, “So that is what it feels like to sit on that swing.”

When you go somewhere you would ordinarily have no reason to visit, some kind of “friction” will certainly arise. Even if that friction is only a light sprinkle, it is a seasoning that completely changes the flavor of an otherwise dull everyday life.

Even if the result is extreme disappointment and an unpleasant experience, that is all right. The things that deeply disappoint us will certainly become useful someday, somewhere.

default.p.n2dokkai-p108.outline.0.label: Introducing the distinction between “things that can be eaten” and “food”
default.p.n2dokkai-p108.outline.0.note: Expresses surprise that almost no one distinguishes between “something that can be eaten” (the biological aspect shared by humanity) and “food” (a socially recognized standard), clarifying that the concept here is considered from the perspective of humanity as a whole, not personal preference.
default.p.n2dokkai-p108.outline.1.label: An analytical example: natto and toxins
default.p.n2dokkai-p108.outline.1.note: Demonstrates that “something that can be eaten” is universal to humanity through natto (foreigners do not die from eating it, so it is edible, but they may not regard it as food), contrasting it with arsenic and potassium cyanide (no one can eat them because they are universally poisonous).
default.p.n2dokkai-p108.outline.2.label: Conclusion: the nature of “food”
default.p.n2dokkai-p108.outline.2.note: Asserts that people in every era and place select items from “things that can be eaten” and rationalize them as their own “food”; “food” is only a very small part of “things that can be eaten.”
default.p.n2dokkai-p108.vietnamese:
What human beings can eat without endangering their lives—that is, “things that are edible”—and what each society recognizes as “food” are different. Surprisingly, almost no one notices this difference. People often confuse the concept of “things that are edible” with whether something is “edible” or “inedible” according to personal preference. However, “edible” and “inedible” here do not refer to personal preferences; they are considered from the perspective of humanity as a whole.

“Things that are edible” are common to all humanity. Whether the Maasai in Kenya eat natto or the French eat natto, their lives would not be endangered. Since the Maasai and the French are human beings just like the Japanese, natto is also a “thing that is edible” for them. At the same time, however, natto is not “food” for them. On the other hand, no one could dissolve arsenic or potassium cyanide in soup and drink it. That is because arsenic and cyanide are not “things that are edible” for humanity as a whole. Such poisonous substances naturally cannot even be considered as “food.”

(Paragraphs omitted)

In every era and every region, people select certain things from among “things that are edible,” give them reasons and meanings, and recognize them as their own “food.” In other words, “food” is only a very small part of “things that are edible.”

Masayuki Nishie, from “An Extracurricular Lesson on ‘Cuisine,’” Heibonsha.

default.p.n2dokkai-p110-g0.vietnamese:
A
In foreign art museums, visitors may take photographs, but in Japanese art museums it is generally not allowed. Perhaps the intention in Japan is for visitors not to become absorbed in taking pictures, but to take their time appreciating the actual works. Recently, smartphone cameras have become increasingly advanced, so even amateurs can take photographs easily. Posting photos on social media is also very popular. If photographers do not disturb people who are quietly viewing the works, shouldn’t photography be allowed? If photography were permitted, people could look at and enjoy their favorite works repeatedly. People who have never visited an art museum before might also begin going. I think this would be a good opportunity for more people to learn about the valuable works held by art museums.

B
At an art museum, I want to spend time appreciating the beauty of the actual works without worrying about taking photographs. I also want to read the explanations of the works carefully. This is often seen in museums that allow photography: people who take pictures seem to focus so much on photographing that they forget to appreciate the works. Some people spend a long time taking pictures right beside a work, then make noise with their friends while looking at the photograph. The sound of smartphone cameras is also unpleasant in a quiet art museum. Moreover, there are copyright issues. It is impossible to control how people will use the photographs they take.

default.p.n2dokkai-p112.vietnamese:
Some of you may already know this, but in 2011 I started an artificial intelligence project called 「Can a Robot Get into the University of Tokyo?」. At that time, there were no other large-scale AI projects in Japan. Since it was a ten-year plan, it has now passed the halfway point and progressed even further. As a result, the project received extensive media coverage under the affectionate name 「Tourobo-kun」 and became widely known. In February 2016, we were also honored to receive the prestigious Netexplo Award. Netexplo is an organization that collects and analyzes information about IT projects around the world and annually selects and honors ten outstanding projects from among thousands in the IT field.

That achievement was certainly something to celebrate, but in reality it also created a difficult problem. Information about the robot attempting to pass the University of Tokyo entrance examination ultimately sent society the misleading message that AI had reached a level at which it could pass the University of Tokyo entrance examination, or was highly likely to do so.

Noriko Arai, 『AI vs. Children Who Cannot Read Textbooks』, Toyo Keizai Shinposha

default.p.n2dokkai-p113.vietnamese:
Although no significant correlation was found between basic reading-comprehension ability and the survey results, one particularly noteworthy finding emerged. There was a strong negative correlation between the rate of school-assistance recipients and ability scores. Article 19 of the School Education Act stipulates: "For the guardians of children or students of school age who are recognized as having difficulty attending school for economic reasons, municipalities must provide the necessary assistance." All children and students identified as needing assistance were receiving school assistance. The survey did not ask whether students received school assistance. We asked the cooperating junior high schools about their school-assistance rates. The results showed that the higher a school's school-assistance rate, the lower its average reading-comprehension score. In other words, poverty is having a negative effect on reading-comprehension ability scores.

(Source: Noriko Arai, "AI versus Children Who Cannot Read Textbooks," Toyo Keizai Shinposha)

default.p.n2dokkai-p114.vietnamese:
Modern society changes so rapidly that it has been called the "age of the second," and we can no longer survive by relying solely on the knowledge we accumulated when we were young. Regardless of age, unless we maintain an "offensive" attitude of continually acquiring new knowledge, we will be left behind by the times.

Furthermore, in a society with an uncertain future, we must also increase our knowledge for the purpose of "self-defense."

Emerging in this age, when people have become so eager for knowledge, is an unprecedented "relearning boom." The number of adults beginning to study continues to rise. Some enter graduate school, some attend cultural or skills programs, and others begin studying to earn qualifications. Whatever their initial reason, I believe it is encouraging that more and more people are beginning to learn.

However, when I observe how people study, I sometimes feel disappointed. This is because they "still have not learned how adults should study."

Studying is not simply memorizing something; it means thinking it over. What matters is expressing and applying externally (outputting) what one has thought about. Taking in knowledge (input), thinking, and then sending it out (output)—I would call this entire process "the way adults learn." Cramming desperately before an examination is merely the forced learning style of children. After taking the trouble to become adults and choosing to study independently, clinging once again to the process of stuffing knowledge in is no different from returning to the old rut.

default.p.n2dokkai-p115-g1.vietnamese:
Working people do not have much time set aside for studying, so they have no choice but to create time for themselves. The first way to create time is through sleep.

During the lunch break, if you doze off at your desk for just five or ten minutes and then wake up refreshed, your mind becomes so clear and alert that you feel you can do anything. Surely you have had an experience like that too, haven't you?

I think the time when people can concentrate best is immediately after a good sleep. You can read faster, and you can write faster. Whatever you do progresses smoothly and efficiently. I call this period “Sweet Time,” or golden time.

Ever since I learned about Sweet Time, I have focused more on the periods when I can concentrate than on the total number of hours I sleep. Rather than deciding how many hours I must sleep each day, I value how many periods of Sweet Time I can create in a day. Compared with staying awake continuously throughout the day, taking occasional short naps increases the total amount of highly focused time overall. The same applies at night. I stay awake until I feel sleepy. I do not set a fixed time when I must go to bed.

default.p.n2dokkai-p116-g0.vietnamese:
【RULES FOR SUBMITTING CONTRIBUTIONS】

"Ganbare! Japanese!" is a Japanese-language magazine for international students, published on the 15th of every month. We are inviting contributions from international students who are readers of the magazine. The rules for submissions are as follows:

＊ The contributor must write the piece personally in Japanese.

＊ Accepted contributions include essays or opinion pieces about your views or experiences, letters to other readers or Japanese people, poetry, haiku, and so on. You may also combine these genres.

＊ The maximum length is 500 characters.

＊ Contributions selected for publication in the magazine may also be posted on our company's website.

＊ Contributors are asked to include their full name, occupation, and contact information (telephone number or email address).

＊ The writer's name will be printed in the magazine. As a rule, contributors should use their real names.

＊ Works that have been published previously may not be submitted.

＊ The editorial staff may make partial revisions to a contribution without changing its content.

＊ If your contribution is published in the magazine, we will send you a copy as a thank-you gift. Therefore, we will ask the selected contributor for a mailing address. You may also decline the gift.

＊ Copyright belongs to "Ganbare! Japanese!" magazine.

Submission address: Contributions Desk, "Ganbare! Japanese!" Publishing

〒123-4567 Post Office Box 1, Tokyo Post Office

Or email: gambarounihongo@toukou.com

◎ The submission deadline is the end of each month. Selected contributions will be published in the issue released on the 15th of the following month. We are unable to answer inquiries about whether a submission has been accepted.

◎ We do not accept illustrations, photographs, writing in languages other than Japanese, writing that hurts others or is discriminatory, or false statements. Please do not write anything untrue.

☆ We look forward to your contributions!!! Ganbare! Japanese!

The Editorial Staff of "Ganbare! Japanese!"

default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.0.label: The perfection of the sound system of American English in children
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.0.note: Explains that the English-American words “mama” and “papa” correspond to M and P sounds, which are among the easiest consonants for infants to pronounce.
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.1.label: The introduction of “mama” into Japan and its physiological rationale
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.1.note: Japanese originally did not use the M sound for "mother," but "mama/papa" quickly became widespread because they suit human speech physiology.
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.2.label: A characteristic of Japanese grammar: it does not emphasize the subject or individual agent
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.2.note: Raises the issue of the word for “mother” in historical Japan and explains that natural Japanese dialogue often omits the subject, so there is no need to explicitly name the individual mother.
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.3.label: Understanding one's mother through words expressing functions and needs
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.outline.3.note: Because of being carried and a close lifestyle, Japanese children perceive their mothers through words expressing basic needs, such as “yum-yum” and “milk,” as people who fulfill those functions.
default.p.n2dokkai-p118.vietnamese:
The English-American children's words 'mama' and 'papa' assign the first voiced consonant, 'M,' that a baby produces unconsciously to the mother, and the first voiceless consonant, 'P,' produced consciously to the father. Among all the sounds in language, these are the two that newborn babies can pronounce most easily. One can only marvel at how ingeniously they came into being.

Japanese, on the other hand, does not assign the sound 'M' to the word for 'mother' (haha). Yet, as everyone knows, the form 'mama' quickly became habitual in Japan.

The roots of 'mama' and 'papa' becoming established cannot be explained simply by the continuous broadcasting of American family dramas on Japanese television in the 1960s. It is because they are wonderful words suited to human physiology. In children's language and in onomatopoeia, we can find many such uses of sounds that fit our sense of things.

Before 'mama' became common in Japan, then, what children's word naturally arose from infants' pronunciation to refer to the mother? In fact, in Japanese—a language in which subjects and objects do not necessarily need to be stated in everyday conversation—there are almost no natural conversational contexts that emphasize the biological individual 'mother.' In Japanese, people do not say, 'Mother, make pudding for me.' Instead, they say, 'Let's make pudding.'

Moreover, because Japanese families have not traditionally hired babysitters and babies are raised in close contact with their mothers through being carried on their backs or held, Japanese infants have few opportunities to perceive their mothers as separate biological individuals. For this reason, Japanese infants first learn words for requesting relief from hunger, discomfort, or anxiety, such as 'munch-munch' or 'pee-pee,' and perceive their mothers as providers of those functions.

default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.0.label: The importance of roads for education
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.0.note: The author raises the issue that road construction in Japan may be criticized, whereas in Ethiopia roads determine people's educational opportunities.
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.1.label: The impact of inadequate roads on teachers and students
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.1.note: Poor roads make teachers unwilling to move to remote areas or cause them to quit; the bad roads make travel expensive, and infrequent vehicles prevent teachers from returning to school on time.
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.2.label: The impact of roads on prices and daily life
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.2.note: Poor roads drive up transportation costs, making all essential goods expensive—something difficult for developed countries to imagine.
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.3.label: Building schools alone is not enough
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.3.note: Donating only to build schools is not enough; a complete system is also needed for teacher training, elementary education, textbook preparation, and teachers' salaries.
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.4.label: Aid and sustainable assistance require many conditions
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.outline.4.note: Aid activities such as digging wells and planting forests are sustainable only when all the necessary conditions are in place; helping others is not simple.
default.p.n2dokkai-p120.vietnamese:
At some point, public projects to build roads in Japan stopped being highly valued. But when you are in Ethiopia, you realize just how important they are. If roads are not properly developed, even opportunities for education will be taken away.

Even if an elementary school is built in a rural area, it will not solve anything if there are no teachers. Since most people who want to become teachers come from cities, it is difficult for them to go to remote places without electricity or roads. Even if they accept a position there, they soon become discouraged and quit.

If roads are not paved, bus fares for shared passenger transportation rise sharply. The number of services also decreases. Simply traveling to town to buy things costs both money and time. Sometimes a child returns from school and says, "Today, the teacher did not come back from town again."

Transportation costs affect the prices of everything. Goods brought from cities become correspondingly expensive because of the long distances and poor roads. Necessities such as clothing and kerosene also become harder to buy. This situation is difficult to imagine for countries with well-developed paved-road systems.

In Japan, there are also calls for donations to build schools in developing countries. However, a building alone is not enough. There must be an organization to train teachers, and primary education to prepare the students who will enter the school is also important. Researchers who can compile textbooks are indispensable as well. A budget to continue paying teachers' salaries is also necessary.

Ethiopia receives a great deal of aid. Whether digging wells or planting forests, sustainable maintenance is possible only when many conditions are met. Helping others is not as simple as it may seem.

Keiichiro Matsumura, "What Is Sustainable Assistance?", The Asahi Shimbun, April 17, 2018.

default.p.n2dokkai-p121-g1.outline.3.label: Origin of the quotation and notes
default.p.n2dokkai-p121-g1.outline.3.note: Source information for the quoted work and an explanation of the new word もじる
default.p.n2dokkai-p121-g1.vietnamese:
To put it in one sentence, today’s forms of media are gradually hiding people’s faces. With a telephone, for example, we can talk without facing the other person. Even so, we can still imagine the other person’s expression from the tone of their voice. With computer networks and email, however, we can no longer even perceive that. The emergence of a multimedia society has opened an era in which we can communicate freely even with people whose faces we have never seen.

For hundreds of thousands of years—or millions, depending on how one counts—from the emergence of human beings, things were not like this. Communicating with another person meant revealing one’s face to that person. To do so, it was best to place one’s face where the other person could see it easily. Even when wearing clothes, the face alone was always left exposed, showing that the presence of the face was the fundamental basis of communication.

However, with the development of various forms of media, communicating without showing one’s face gradually became normal. I call this an “anonymous communication society.” “Anonymous” means hiding one’s face, and naturally it is a newly coined word modeled on the word “anonymous.”

原島博『顔学への招待』岩波科学ライブラリー (Hiroshi Harashima, “An Invitation to Facial Studies,” Iwanami Scientific Library)

default.p.n2dokkai-p122.vietnamese:
A

Traffic accidents caused by drivers aged 70 and over are becoming a serious problem. I think a rule should be introduced requiring everyone with a driver’s license to surrender it upon turning 70. One survey found that the older drivers become, the more confident they are in their driving ability, but even if their skills are good, their physical functions have declined and their reflexes have slowed. It must be regrettable to give up driving after many years behind the wheel, but please try imagining yourself becoming the person responsible for causing a traffic accident.

After surrendering their licenses, people may face different circumstances depending on the region, but services have been prepared to prevent their lives from becoming inconvenient, such as half-price bus fares and discounted taxi fares. Therefore, they only need to take advantage of these services.

B

Although we commonly refer to them as elderly drivers, driving ability differs from person to person. Some people drive poorly even when they are young, while others still drive very skillfully despite being elderly. Requiring everyone to surrender their license upon reaching a certain age is a rigid, mechanical rule. Instead, people should be required to undergo a cognitive-function test at a medical facility every six months from around the age of 60. Those whom a doctor determines to be "dangerous drivers" through this testing would have to surrender their licenses. Those who are elderly but have no problems with driving should still be allowed to drive.

In reality, local-government services for people who can no longer drive are still inadequate. The services needed differ between major cities with well-developed public transportation and regional cities where cars are the main means of transportation.

default.p.n2dokkai-p124.vietnamese:
[Paragraph 1]
Technology should be evaluated according to the following three points: (1) whether it enriches the lives of its users, (2) whether it is highly compatible with its users, and (3) whether it is highly compatible with the environment in which its users live.

[Paragraph 2]
Since the Industrial Revolution, technology has continually enriched our lives. Engines enhance our muscular strength, enabling us to generate great force easily. Telescopes and microscopes enhance our eyesight, allowing us to see distant objects and tiny objects. Computers enhance the power of our brains, enabling us to perform complex calculations quickly and process large amounts of stored data.

[Paragraph 3]
The fact that these technologies have enriched our lives is undeniable. However, it is also true that we have reached the point where we must reconsider the traditional way of evaluating technology, which has focused solely on the perspective of enriching users’ lives. An automobile, for example, is a fairly highly developed technology by traditional standards, but when its compatibility with people and the environment is taken into account, it can be said to remain a very immature technology.

[Paragraph 4]
From the perspective of compatibility with people, nothing is better than a tool being a natural extension of the hands, feet, eyes, or mind. If the operating principles of a tool and a person are the same, compatibility will improve. Unfortunately, computers and engines operate according to principles completely different from those of the brain and muscles. That is why they are difficult to control. The [      ] itself is probably evidence that automobiles are still an unfinished technology.

[Paragraph 5]
The issue of compatibility between the environment and automobiles has traditionally been discussed in connection with air pollution. However, as discussed here, automobiles are inherently incapable of operating unless the environment is made completely flat. A technology that cannot operate unless it first completely changes the environment in which its users live can hardly be called a superior technology.

Tatsuo Motokawa, excerpt from “The Time of Elephants, the Time of Mice,” Chuokoron-Shinsha

default.p.n2dokkai-p126.vietnamese:
A large body has the advantage of making an animal less susceptible to environmental influences and enabling it to maintain its independence. Animals interact with the environment through their body surfaces. The larger the size, the smaller the surface area per unit of volume, so it can be understood that larger animals are less affected by the environment through their body surfaces.

Body temperature is a typical example of this. The larger an organism is, the more easily it can maintain a constant body temperature. This follows the same principle as hot water in a small bowl cooling very quickly, while hot water in a bathtub takes time to heat but also cools very slowly. Volume is proportional to the cube of length, whereas surface area is proportional to the square of length. Therefore, the ratio of <surface area / volume> is inversely proportional to length, or size, and gradually decreases. A large bathtub has a relatively smaller area in contact with the cold air outside than a bowl of water does. That is why it cools slowly. If we apply this reasoning, larger animals are probably better able to withstand sudden changes in the environmental temperature.

Maintaining a stable body temperature has an even greater advantage. The speed of chemical reactions occurring in the body varies with temperature, and the higher the temperature, the faster the reactions proceed. Muscle contraction naturally also depends on chemical reactions, so the speed of muscle contraction differs according to temperature. Therefore, even if an animal reaches out its hand at exactly the right moment as before, if its body temperature has fallen compared with earlier, it will miss its prey. This is extremely disadvantageous.

Tatsuo Motokawa, "Elephant Time, Mouse Time," Chuokoron-Shinsha

default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.0.label: Changes in the standards for evaluating people in Japan
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.0.note: After 25 years of involvement, the author has noticed that Japanese standards for evaluating people have changed considerably.
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.1.label: American influence and the author's sadness
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.1.note: Japanese people have been influenced by the United States and now place too much emphasis on evaluating results, contrary to what originally made the author admire Japan.
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.2.label: The experience of being unable to adapt to American culture
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.2.note: While working in the United States, the author came to understand how Americans value results and felt unable to adapt to this attitude.
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.3.label: The nature of results-based evaluation in the United States
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.outline.3.note: Explains this specifically through an American proverb: a person's results and value are measured only in monetary terms.
default.p.n2dokkai-p127.vietnamese:
Having been involved with Japan for nearly a quarter of a century, I feel that Japanese standards for evaluating people have changed considerably. I feel that the basis on which people judge someone when they meet them has changed greatly compared with the past.

In terms of how things have changed, I feel that people have come to place too much importance on judging people by their “results,” influenced by the United States—especially the United States from the Reagan era onward—and this makes me very sad. The reason I first came to Japan and thought, “Ah, this is the country that suits me best,” was that I believed the standards for evaluating people here were different from those in other countries, especially the United States.

At that time, every year I spent several months living and working at a research institute in the United States. During those years, I deeply realized that the standard for evaluating people in that country was “results,” and I also felt that I could not adapt to it.

To explain what it means to evaluate people by their results, there is a famous saying in the United States: “If you're so smart, why aren't you rich?” In other words, if you say you are so smart, why don't you have any money now? If you were really smart, you should have made money by now. That is what it means. They believe that a person's value can be measured only by their current results, and the standard for measuring those results is money. I feel that in this country, people without money are not regarded as worthy of much respect.

Peter Frankl, “Peter’s Advice on How to Live,” Iwanami Junior Shinsho.

default.p.n2dokkai-p128.vietnamese:
A

Parks are places where many people gather: mothers letting their young children play, elderly people taking walks, and people jogging. Parks are also places for social interaction, where people enjoy chatting while eating boxed lunches or drinking tea. Festivals are sometimes held there, and children sometimes come for outings. At such times, it would be very inconvenient if there were nowhere to throw away trash.

It is true that cleaning up and disposing of trash requires both labor and money. However, it is said that since trash cans were removed, complaints from residents about empty lunch boxes and plastic bottles being scattered around parks and in the bushes along the surrounding sidewalks have been increasing. If parks had trash cans, people would throw their trash into them. Wouldn't that save both effort and money instead?

B

How do people dispose of their trash when they go to the mountains or the beach? Most people surely take it home, because there are no trash cans there. In other words, whenever people see a trash can, they throw things into it. From this perspective, removing trash cans from parks is considered natural. Food waste in particular becomes food for crows and rats, so leaving it there for several days is very unsanitary. It produces bad odors and may cause dissatisfaction among park users.

In addition, who should bear the cost of disposing of the trash? Events in particular would surely require a large amount of money. Is it reasonable to place that burden entirely on the local government? I think each person should take their own trash home and dispose of it where they live. Since no one wants to carry bulky trash home, wouldn't this ultimately help reduce the amount of waste as well?

default.p.n2dokkai-p130.vietnamese:
I have taught university students for 23 years. Since I belong to an engineering department, all of my students are in the sciences. They are certainly good at mathematics and physics compared with average students. Occasionally, students from other departments also came to attend my lectures, and I was also in charge of seminars for students in the humanities and social sciences. In those classes, participants took turns giving presentations and discussing them rather than simply listening to a lecture. I always encouraged students to ask questions. I even established a rule that every student had to ask at least one question in each class. In addition, in lectures attended by about 100 people, I handed out slips of paper every time and required everyone to submit a question. I typed those questions using a word processor and wrote an answer to each one. I printed the material and distributed it to everyone at the next lecture. This allowed students to learn what everyone else besides themselves had asked. I did this every time.

Having doubts, asking questions, or, in other words, discovering problems, is extremely important to science. No, not only to science. In every field, we must continually strive to find out where the problems lie. It can be said that this attitude moves everything forward. This means that it is not enough to wait for a problem to arise and then solve it. Put more radically, anyone can solve problems. There are hardly any problems in this world that are so difficult that they cannot be solved. Because experience has accumulated over the past, most problems have already been incorporated into procedural manuals. Even when there are difficulties such as inconvenience, technical complexity, or expense, there are very few problems for which we cannot think of even one solution. It may not be an exaggeration to say that 99% of problems can be solved mechanically.

What is difficult is discovering the problem. Identifying where the problem lies is the most important task, and that is what requires human ability.

Therefore, [ B ] requires much more thinking than [ A ].

Hiroshi Mori, "What Does It Mean to Be Scientific?", Gentosha.

default.p.n2dokkai-p132.outline.0.note: Provides comparative figures: languages number approximately 3,000–7,000, whereas writing systems number only about 400.

default.p.n2dokkai-p132.outline.2.label: Why the number of writing systems is smaller than the number of languages: the existence of languages without writing systems
default.p.n2dokkai-p132.outline.2.note: Explains that many languages are spoken but have no written form, resulting in societies without writing.
default.p.n2dokkai-p132.vietnamese:
It is extremely difficult to calculate exactly how many languages people speak in total. However, according to one linguist's statistics, approximately 7,000 languages have existed throughout history, while only about 3,000 are currently spoken on Earth (there are also many different theories on this matter). When it comes to writing systems used to express these languages, however, the number decreases dramatically, and is estimated to be only about 400.

Moreover, this figure of 400 includes writing systems that have not yet been fully deciphered, such as ancient scripts like the Egyptian hieroglyphs, the Mesopotamian cuneiform inscriptions carved into clay tablets, the Khitan script used by the Khitan dynasty in northern China (916–1125), and the Maya script used by the Maya civilization, which flourished from the sixth century onward across Mexico and Central America. In other words, the total number of writing systems that have ever existed, across all times and places, is estimated to be about 400.

There is naturally a reason why the number of writing systems is only about one-tenth the number of languages. One reason is that there are “languages with no writing system of their own.” Regardless of the language in question, even if there are “languages that have a____ but not b____,” the reverse case—“languages that have c____ but not d____”—does not exist at all. In places where languages without writing systems are spoken, what is known as a “non-literate society” develops.

default.p.n2dokkai-p134.vietnamese:
A
At hospitals in Japan, there are often cases in which patients have to wait a very long time before being seen. In places with long waits, people reportedly sometimes have to wait three or four hours. This is truly painful for patients who are already feeling unwell.
To address this situation, the internal-medicine department at Hospital A introduced an Internet appointment system. Patients enter their name and patient ID on the appointment website and then select their desired time slot. Patients are required to arrive at the hospital 30 minutes before their appointment. Appointments are limited to consultations on the same day.
However, if an emergency patient needs priority treatment, the consultation time will naturally be delayed. In addition, only people who can connect to the Internet can use this system. Although many problems remain, the hospital can be said to be making efforts to reduce overcrowding by shortening waiting times, even if only for some patients.

B
At the dermatology department of Hospital B, patients have to wait up to four hours to be seen on Saturdays. Even on weekdays, waiting for more than two hours is normal. Usually, one would think that some measure should be taken to improve this situation.
However, in dermatology, very few patients are so seriously ill that they cannot walk around. Patients ask about the waiting time in advance, go out during the time before their turn, and return at the appropriate time to read or do something else. Patients who want to go out only need to inform the reception desk in advance, and they are required to return 30 minutes before the time they are told. If an appointment system were introduced, patients might easily expect to be seen exactly at that time. Therefore, perhaps the hospital wants patients to wait patiently and make useful use of their time in their own way.

default.p.n2dokkai-p14-g1.vietnamese:
It is said that Japanese people's faces have been gradually changing in recent years. Apparently, faces used to be square, but are now gradually becoming more like inverted triangles. The reason is said to be changes in food.

Thinking about it, people in the past often ate hard foods such as senbei rice crackers and dried squid, even as snacks, whereas today there are more soft foods such as cookies and ice cream. Over a long period of time, it is said that the farther back people lived, the larger their jawbones were. If this trend continues, Japanese people's faces will probably continue to change in the future.

default.p.n2dokkai-p15-g1.vietnamese:
Dolphins are mammals like humans, but they have adapted to life underwater and cannot live on land. However, because they cannot breathe through gills like fish, dolphins must regularly raise the blowholes on top of their heads above the water to breathe.

For this reason, if a dolphin were to sleep completely soundly, it would drown. However, dolphins do sleep. They swim slowly near the surface while alternately closing one eye at a time every few minutes, allowing each half of the brain to rest. Although this is far from what we would call a good night’s sleep, they apparently manage to sleep by repeating this process more than 300 times a day.

Tadaaki Imaizumi, editor, “A Dictionary of Regrettable Creatures,” Takahashi Publishing.

The results of a recent survey on the average amount of time university students spend reading and using smartphones have been published, revealing the following:

According to a 1973 survey, students spent 99 minutes reading, but by 2014 that time had decreased by nearly 70 minutes. The percentage of university students who spent 0 minutes reading rose from 3% to 41%, while the percentage who read for 60 minutes or more but less than 90 minutes fell from 29% to 16%. In addition, according to another survey, the average time spent reading newspapers also fell from 40 minutes in 1973 to just 10 minutes in 2005.

In contrast, students are reported to spend 163 minutes a day using smartphones. By gender, women (2 hours 57 minutes) tended to spend more time using them than men (2 hours 32 minutes). The percentage of students who did not own a smartphone and reported spending 0 minutes using one was 4%.

default.p.n2dokkai-p20-g0.vietnamese:
【Person Seeking Advice】
I am an international student currently attending a university in Japan. Six months ago, I made a friend my age through an exchange event with Japanese people. She is a very nice person. Since being friends with her has also helped me study Japanese, I thought how lucky I was. However, recently I have been receiving a lot of messages from her every day. They are not about anything important, just things like "Good morning," "I'm eating lunch now," and "I just bought this XX," and so on. University studies are very busy, and replying to messages in Japanese is not easy for me at all. I would like to reduce our back-and-forth messaging, but how can I communicate that without seeming rude?

【Respondent A】
Short messages are not much of a burden for Japanese people, are they? But I understand that they are difficult for an international student. If you tell your friend, "My Japanese isn't very good yet, so I can't reply right away. Please be understanding!", the messages may decrease a little.

【Respondent B】
It is certainly difficult to reply in Japanese, which is a foreign language. However, although it may feel difficult at first, even sending a short reply is a great opportunity to learn the practical Japanese used by young people your age. Try thinking of it as Japanese practice and enjoying it.

default.p.n2dokkai-p21.vietnamese:
Surely everyone knows the difference between a use-by date and a best-before date. The use-by date is the date after which something should no longer be eaten, while the best-before date indicates how long it can be enjoyed at its best. So, did you know that frozen foods also have best-before dates? They vary from product to product, but they are generally about one to one and a half years.

Frozen foods sold on the market are frozen extremely quickly at a low temperature of between −30 and −40°C. As a result, their flavor does not deteriorate, their nutritional value is not lost, and they can be preserved for a long time. However, they must be stored below −18°C. Although the freezer compartment of a household refrigerator is kept at around −18°C, the temperature rises every time the door is opened. This causes the quality to decline, so frozen food should be eaten as soon as possible; if possible, eat it within 3 to 4 months. Refreezing food after it has thawed once is also very undesirable.

In addition, when food is frozen at home, it cannot be frozen quickly, so compared with commercially sold products, [ ... ]. It is recommended that you finish eating it within about 1 month.

What should we do if a fire breaks out at home or at work? A small fire can be extinguished with a fire extinguisher, but if the flames rise higher than 1 meter, escape immediately.

The important thing then is to shout loudly first to alert people nearby that there is a fire, and be sure to close the door. If you do not, the smoke will follow you at an extremely high speed. Since we do not know where a fire will break out, memorize several escape routes in advance and check them from time to time. It is extremely dangerous to leave objects blocking an emergency exit. Also, never use an elevator.

Carbon monoxide (CO) in smoke is a colorless, odorless gas; inhaling it causes CO poisoning. In fire accidents, many people actually die for this reason. CO is lighter than air, so lower your body when evacuating.

default.p.n2dokkai-p25.vietnamese:
Self-driving vehicles have five levels of automation, from Level 1 to Level 5, as shown in the table on the right. Among them, vehicles equipped with Level 1 automatic braking are already widely available to the public. Level 2 vehicles are also being sold in some places. ( 1 ), because driver supervision is still required at Levels 1 and 2, a vehicle must be Level 3 or higher to truly be called “self-driving.”

The most important thing in automated driving is “not hitting people.” ( 2 ), the first step is to train AI (artificial intelligence) to recognize what kinds of objects are people. Then, the system is programmed to judge when sensors or cameras mounted on the vehicle detect a person and apply the brakes.

Having self-driving vehicles operate on highways where there are no pedestrians is [ A ]. ( 3 ), on ordinary roads, where unpredictable events such as someone suddenly running into the road can occur, the challenges that must be solved increase greatly.

For example, in a test conducted in the United States in March 2018 in which a vehicle [ B ] was driven, the AI judged during autonomous driving that emergency braking was necessary, but the human driver failed to react in time, resulting in an accident.

default.p.n2dokkai-p29.vietnamese:
「Children's Cafés」, which have been spreading in recent years, provide meals for children who do not receive adequate nutrition during their growing years for economic reasons, or who have to eat alone every day because their parents work constantly. At a 「Children's Café」, children can happily enjoy a warm, healthy meal together with others.

Unlike ordinary restaurants, these places are operated largely by volunteers. Each meal costs a few hundred yen, and in some cases it is free. Some of the ingredients are also donated by local residents, shops, and businesses. In some cases, the local government helps cover utility and rent costs. People who believe that children should not be allowed to suffer are joining forces to help.

「Children's Cafés」 serve another purpose besides providing meals.

There is always someone present at a 「Children's Café」. Children can talk about what they did at school that day, and someone will listen to them. At these places, they experience things that many children would ordinarily experience at home. Through such experiences, children learn about connections between people. That is why they do not go home immediately after eating, but stay to do their homework. Recently, adults in the neighborhood have also begun connecting with one another, gradually turning these places into lively community gathering spots.

default.p.n2dokkai-p30-g1.vietnamese:
Recently, I have felt that more and more people are using 「お父さんが」 (my father) and 「お母さんが」 (my mother) when talking to others about their own parents. This way of speaking gives an extremely childish impression. They should appropriately say 「父が」 and 「母が」 (my father/my mother). When I hear sentences such as “Your father helped me the other day. Thank you very much,” I am startled. I have also heard people say 「お姉さんが」 and 「お兄さんが」 in situations where they should say 「姉」 and 「兄」. In contrast, I have sometimes heard the news refer to other people’s parents as 「父」 and 「母」, as in “Person A’s father...” or “Person B’s mother...”

Is this because people do not understand the Japanese distinction between uchi and soto, or is it a change toward no longer distinguishing between those boundaries? If so, what is ultimately the reason for this loss of distinction?

default.p.n2dokkai-p31-g0.outline.1.note: Points out a subjective human tendency: an item priced cheaply and reduced by 50% seems like a great bargain, whereas an expensive item reduced by only 1% does not seem much different.
default.p.n2dokkai-p31-g0.outline.2.label: Shifting one’s perspective to the actual amount of money and the author’s behavior
default.p.n2dokkai-p31-g0.outline.2.note: The author reminds readers to focus on the actual amount saved—10,000 yen versus 500 yen—and consequently changes the habit of concentrating only on controlling large expenses.
default.p.n2dokkai-p31-g0.outline.3.label: The central conclusion about cutting costs
default.p.n2dokkai-p31-g0.outline.3.note: The core conclusion is that when cutting costs, one must think in terms of absolute amounts rather than percentages.
default.p.n2dokkai-p31-g0.vietnamese:
① Buy a 1,000-yen item for 500 yen.
② Buy a 1.01-million-yen item for 1 million yen.
Which of these two examples is the better deal?

Buying a 1,000-yen item for 500 yen makes us feel as though we have gotten twice the value. Indeed, in percentage terms, it is a 50% discount.

In contrast, when buying a 1.01-million-yen item for 1 million yen, the discount is only about 1%, and in terms of the price, 1.01 million yen and 1 million yen do not feel very different.

However, let us calmly think about it—the actual saving is as much as 10,000 yen! When faced with that amount, a 500-yen difference in profit or loss is no longer important.

That is why I ignored the profit or loss on purchases under 10,000 yen and intervened only in large purchases.

Thus, cost reduction should not be considered in terms of percentages; it should be considered in terms of absolute amounts.

Shinya Yamada, 『Why Doesn’t the Clothesline Shop Go Bankrupt?』 / Kobunsha Shinsho

default.p.n2dokkai-p32.vietnamese:
The number of working women is steadily increasing. Looking at the graph showing the labor-force participation rate, we can see that its shape has changed from an “M” shape to an inverted “U” shape. In 1986, when the Equal Employment Opportunity Law for Men and Women※ took effect, the graph formed an M-shaped curve: the labor-force participation rate declined during the period of marriage and childbirth, then rose again once child-rearing had stabilized.

According to the Labor Force Survey released by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications on January 30, 2017, the decline among people in their 30s—corresponding to the bottom of the M—had become gentler. Labor-force participation rates also increased across the board from the age of 40 onward. (The rest is omitted.)

January 30, 2018 — Nihon Keizai Shimbun

default.p.n2dokkai-p34-g1.vietnamese:
Children’s unaided visual acuity—their eyesight measured without glasses—is declining. Even among elementary school students, more than 30% have visual acuity below the normal standard of 1.0, and by middle school the figure exceeds 50%. Compared with 20 years ago, these figures have increased approximately twofold and 1.6-fold, respectively. Surprisingly, this increase began around the same time smartphones became widespread.

That is not all. Recently, the term “smartphone presbyopia” has also appeared. Presbyopia is a condition in which what one is looking at becomes blurry or nearby objects become difficult to see. It usually results from aging, but continuously focusing on nearby objects, as when using a smartphone or playing games, is also said to be a cause.

default.p.n2dokkai-p35-g1.vietnamese: When talking about earthquakes, the terms “seismic intensity” (shindo) and “magnitude” are commonly used. The former indicates how strongly the ground is shaking in a particular area, and the farther an area is from the “epicenter,” where the earthquake originated, the weaker the shaking becomes. Seismic intensity is divided into 10 levels. For example, at seismic intensity 3, “most people feel the shaking if they are not moving,” while at seismic intensity 4, “hanging objects such as electric lights shake strongly,” and so on. Magnitude, on the other hand, is a numerical value indicating the size of the earthquake itself and represents the amount of energy released by it. Earthquakes range from extremely small ones below M1 to enormous ones of M8 or higher, and when the magnitude differs by 1, the energy increases 32-fold.

default.p.n2dokkai-p36.vietnamese:
The way convenience stores operate may change. This is because keeping stores open 24 hours a day—once a symbol of convenience stores—is becoming increasingly difficult due to factors such as labor shortages. It is becoming impossible to secure enough night-shift workers to support 24-hour operations, and the number of stores struggling to maintain them is increasing. (Passage omitted) It is not uncommon for store managers to work long hours to make up for staff shortages. (Passage omitted)

More than 90% of convenience stores are operated by individual business owners. These are store owners who have signed membership agreements (called “franchise agreements”) with headquarters to become part of a chain.

Headquarters grants the stores permission to use its brand name and sell products developed by headquarters. In return, the stores are required to pay headquarters a certain amount based on their profits.

Because the more a store’s sales increase, the more money headquarters receives from it, headquarters wants stores to extend their business hours. Customers also find stores convenient when they are always open. However, in a nationwide public-opinion survey conducted by the Mainichi Shimbun in March, as many as 79% of respondents said that 24-hour opening should be reconsidered.

Nevertheless, stores now want to shorten their business hours because of labor shortages. According to a survey by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, 60% of store owners said they were experiencing staff shortages. The ministry has asked major convenience-store chains to draw up plans (passage omitted) to improve conditions for stores.

default.p.n2dokkai-p39.outline.1.label: Distinguishing visible oil from invisible oil
default.p.n2dokkai-p39.outline.1.note: The passage defines and classifies two types of fats: visible fats, such as cooking oil and butter, and invisible fats naturally contained in foods such as meat, fish, grains, and instant foods.

default.p.n2dokkai-p39.vietnamese:
Because they believe that “fat makes you fat,” some people limit their use of vegetable oil and salad dressing. In terms of energy, fat contains more calories (9 kcal per gram) than carbohydrates and protein (4 kcal per gram each), so consuming the same amount makes it easier to gain weight. Fat also contains nutrients essential to our bodies, so instead of restricting it excessively, we need to find ways to avoid consuming too much.

There are visible fats and invisible fats. Oils used in cooking, such as vegetable oil, butter, margarine, and mayonnaise, are visible fats. Invisible fats are fats naturally present in foods themselves, such as meat, fish, grains, beans, dairy products, confectionery, and instant noodles.

Invisible fats are very difficult to recognize by ourselves when we consume them. Of the fat consumed by Japanese people, visible fat accounts for two parts (20%), while invisible fat accounts for approximately eight parts (80%). Therefore, it is very important to control the amount of invisible fat.

For fatty cuts of meat, cooking methods such as grilling or steaming can help limit fat intake. For seasoning, salt, soy sauce, miso, vinegar, ponzu sauce, and oil-free dressings are good choices.

default.p.n2dokkai-p40.vietnamese:
Critic Toshio Okada wrote a book titled “Don’t Stay Fat Forever.” Apparently, Mr. Okada used to be very overweight, but lost as much as 50 kilograms in one year. His experience at that time is described in this book. Drawing on his experience of dieting and losing weight, Mr. Okada explains the difference between “desire” and “need.” Both words mean “wanting to have something” or “wanting to do something,” but he analyzes the difference in their meanings as follows.

First, try to imagine someone who is very overweight. How do you think such a person eats? They do not eat because they are hungry. Instead, they eat because they think, “I want to eat that cake I saw on TV,” or “I want to eat at the restaurant that opened last week.” They are always eating. He calls this the “desire type.” Mr. Okada does not say that people of the “desire type” are bad. On the contrary, apparently most of them are healthy and energetic. Next, try to think about a thin person. A thin person is the “need type,” meaning that they eat only after recognizing the hunger signals sent by their body. They do not eat because a food was introduced on TV or because a restaurant has a long line. He says that people like this often seem calm and refined.

Apparently, if you can control both desire and need, your diet will be successful.

default.p.n2dokkai-p41.vietnamese:
【Questioner】
Japanese people often ask me, “What surprised you or did you find difficult when you came to Japan?” Since I can generally understand everyday Japanese, I do not have much difficulty communicating. However, one troublesome part of daily life is sorting garbage. I am still not used to separating glass bottles, cans, plastic bottles, plastic items, paper, metal, batteries, bulky waste, and so on. In my country, we do not need to sort garbage at all; we simply throw everything away, and we can do so at any time. After we throw out the garbage, someone else sorts it, and they do all the work. Because I am busy studying for exams, I really feel that sorting garbage is a burden. I wish there were people in Japan responsible for sorting garbage as well.

【Respondent A】
I feel the same way. If I am busy on the designated garbage-collection day, I cannot take out the garbage, and it piles up in my room. I sometimes think sorting garbage is a nuisance. On top of that, the sorting rules differ depending on the local area, which is confusing, isn't it? However, if we have other people do the sorting, it will cost an enormous amount of time and money. That cost comes from taxes. I think it is best for each of us to make a small effort to sort our own garbage.

【Respondent B】
Sorting garbage means separating recyclable items from non-recyclable items. I think reducing the amount of waste and recycling it helps conserve resources and protect the environment. We should not think only of ourselves; why not regard it as a responsibility to our children, grandchildren, and future generations? The waste we produce every day is directly connected to environmental issues.

default.p.n2dokkai-p42-g1.vietnamese:
Differences in size can be seen between animals living on islands and those living on continents. A typical example is the elephant: isolated on islands, elephants have gradually become smaller over many generations. Since islands generally have less food and less space than continents, it may seem easy to understand why animals would become smaller to adapt. However, the situation is not that simple. When we look at small animals such as mice and rabbits, we find that, in contrast, they become increasingly larger on islands.

（Tatsuo Motokawa, 'Elephant Time, Mouse Time', Chuokoron-Shinsha）

default.p.n2dokkai-p43-g0.vietnamese:
Person A: I think a surname is merely a label, so being overly particular about it is strange. It is only something inherited from one's parents, after all. If my fiancée is an only child and wants to keep her surname, I would have no problem changing mine.

Person B: My husband's parents and siblings treat me as one of their family, but I think that is because I share a surname with my parents-in-law. I hope the new law will also include a provision allowing people who currently use their spouse's surname to change back to their original surname.

Person C: I want to continue working throughout my life, so I want to preserve the reputation I have built under my current name.
