default.p.n2dokkai-p44.outline.0.label: Differences by birth month and two patterns of development
default.p.n2dokkai-p44.outline.0.note: Provides statistics on track-and-field athletes: childhood performance does not determine the future, and differences caused by birth month in childhood disappear in adulthood.
default.p.n2dokkai-p44.outline.1.label: Problems with early training and its two negative consequences
default.p.n2dokkai-p44.outline.1.note: Points out that selecting only highly gifted students early for intensive training harms both late developers, who are overlooked, and early developers, who stagnate and face pressure.
default.p.n2dokkai-p44.outline.2.label: Advice to diversify one’s sports and solutions adopted by various countries
default.p.n2dokkai-p44.outline.2.note: The passage advises children to experience many activities instead of being forced to specialize in only one, citing countries such as Germany that have abolished nationwide junior-high-school competitions.
default.p.n2dokkai-p44.vietnamese:
Among the athletes representing Japan in track and field, only one in five had ever placed in the top eight at the national junior-high-school championships. This means that some athletes are early bloomers who run very fast from elementary school, while others are late bloomers whose performance improves after high school.

Looking at the birth months of athletes who competed in national track-and-field championships, at the elementary-school level, there were far more people born from April to June than those born from January to March—the “early-born” children, who are physically developing nearly a year later. As age increases, this trend gradually weakens, and among Japanese athletes representing the country at the Olympics or World Championships, almost no difference remains according to birth month.

However, in actual sports training, this background is not adequately taken into account, and only elementary-school students with good results receive specialized intensive training from an early age. One professor points out that this involves two problems.

“The hidden talent of late-blooming athletes may go unrecognized and be buried. Conversely, among early bloomers, some stop developing at an early stage, fail to improve as expected, and become troubled and distressed.”

The professor also says that during elementary and junior high school, it is important not to narrow a child’s focus to one specialized sport but to enjoy a wide variety of sports. This is because during those years, it is impossible to know which sport a child is talented at or suited to.

Even so, because the goal of becoming number one in Japan is so attractive, people still want to specialize in one sport by any means possible. Therefore, in order to [        ], some countries, such as Germany, have reportedly abolished national competitions for junior-high-school students.

(Excerpted and partially adapted from the April 2019 issue of Gekkan Junior Aera, published by Asahi Shimbun)

Mr. A, formerly a bank employee, married a woman he had met through work. Two years later, their child was born, and he began taking action to realize a long-held dream: leaving his job and starting a career in agriculture ("shunou").

Shunou means starting farming as an occupation, and in most cases it involves leaving one's previous job before beginning agriculture. Mr. A was drawn to the process of experimenting and creating crops from tiny seeds, and during every vacation he traveled to different places, wondering what it would be like to farm. Despite his anxieties, he eventually decided to move to a village in Gunma Prefecture.

There, young couples who wished to begin farming were accepted and could take part in a one-year training program. The training included instructors, chiefly elderly farmers who had farmed all their lives, and learning how to prepare the soil properly...

default.p.n2dokkai-p48-g0.vietnamese:
In the past, a friend of mine who was expanding a business involving several restaurants in the Tokyo area confided in me.

My friend said that employees had asked, “＿＿＿＿＿＿＿＿?” but that he did not know how to answer appropriately.

So I suggested that he try giving them an example by analogy, as follows.

I said, “If the world’s wealthiest and most discerning gourmet came to dine at the restaurant, how would you have to serve them to make them satisfied?”

“If the customer were the world’s wealthiest and most discerning gourmet, they would certainly have already tasted all the dishes considered the best around the world. From French and Italian cuisine to Spanish and Chinese cuisine... Whenever there was a delicious dish in season, they would surely fly in their private plane to a restaurant in that country to eat it. If they wanted to eat something for lunch, they might fly by helicopter directly to that restaurant.

It would be impossible to satisfy someone like that through ingredients or food alone, because they already eat the best food in the world. Then what should we do? Surely, the only way to satisfy them would be through the quality of the service,” I said.

For every customer to feel, “I’m glad I came to this restaurant,” the quality of the food alone is not enough; the quality of the service is the crucial factor.

(芳中晃『女性がディズニーランドに何度も行ってしまう理由』中経出版 - Akira Yoshinaka, excerpt from 『Why Women Keep Going to Disneyland』, Chukei Publishing)

default.p.n2dokkai-p51-g0.vietnamese: Secondhand stores are very popular these days. Unlike in the past, they look stylish and fashionable, and whenever I stop by, they are full of people buying used goods to save money and people selling belongings to help protect the environment. So I decided to try selling something too, and first brought in ten items of clothing. When I asked them to appraise them, they said the total was 400 yen. Although I knew perfectly well that the store had to resell them for a profit, I still thought, “Is that all?” The next time I sold books, they bought five books for 1,000 yen. When I asked why, they told me that an old insect dictionary was worth 700 yen because it contained pictures of insects that apparently had become extinct, and some people wanted to buy it. It seems that this world is full of surprising discoveries.

default.p.n2dokkai-p51-g1.vietnamese: Have you ever heard of the World Expo, commonly shortened to Expo (万博)? It is a major event that brings together countries from around the world to showcase the latest scientific technologies and promote their countries according to various themes. It can be held only after an application is submitted to the Bureau International des Expositions and approved by its General Assembly. There are two types of Expo: the large-scale type, called a "Registered Exhibition," and the smaller type, called a "Recognized Exhibition." The former is held once every 5 years, while the latter is held in between them. The duration is also specifically regulated: the former lasts up to 6 months, while the latter lasts up to 3 months. default.p.n2dokkai-p57-g1.vietnamese:
【 Furthermore / In conclusion / Then / However 】

Japan is famous around the world as a country with a long life expectancy. （1: Then）, which prefectures in Japan have the greatest number of long-lived elderly people? Surely, many people would think that prefectures with a mild climate—neither too cold nor too hot—would be the places where people live the longest. Until fairly recently, that was indeed the case. （2: However）, recently, it seems that this can no longer always be said to be true.

According to news reports from 2017, Shiga Prefecture ranked first for men, Nagano Prefecture second, and Kyoto Prefecture third. For women, Nagano Prefecture ranked first, followed by Okayama and Shimane prefectures. Except for Okayama, all of these prefectures have low winter temperatures, （3: furthermore）, they receive a great deal of snow. （4: In conclusion）, it can be said that climate alone is not the factor that determines life expectancy.

default.p.n2dokkai-p60-g1.vietnamese:
Vinegar can broadly be divided into two types: rice vinegar and fruit vinegar. In Asia, including Japan, rice vinegar is predominant, whereas fruit vinegar is more common in Western Europe. Why is there such a regional difference?

In fact, people generally use vinegar made from the same ingredient as the type of alcohol commonly consumed in that region. For example, Japanese sake is made from rice, and, naturally, rice vinegar is also made from rice. In contrast, wine is widely consumed in France and Italy, and wine vinegar, made from grapes, plays an important role in cooking. Incidentally, in Germany and England—the homelands of beer—malt vinegar made from malt extract is very popular, while in the United States, apple cider vinegar is common. Thus, the alcohol and vinegar of each region are closely connected.

The reason is extremely simple. If alcoholic beverages such as wine are left as they are, bacteria multiply, causing fermentation and transforming them into vinegar. In this way, vinegar was discovered by chance in various places and gradually came to be widely used in cooking.

Vinegar has a very long history. Records remain showing that it was produced in ancient Babylon around 5000 B.C., and it is regarded as the oldest seasoning in the world. Vinegar appears in Japanese writings around the fourth or fifth century, and its production method was transmitted from China. It spread among ordinary people during the Edo period. Vinegar...

default.p.n2dokkai-p62.vietnamese:
As I continuously gathered information about famous sightseeing spots in central Tokyo from tour guides who showed foreign visitors around and concierges at hotels, I heard many surprising stories. There were countless examples of visitors targeting places that people like us who live in Tokyo did not consider particularly valuable, or places whose existence we had not known about at all. Apparently, even the guides frequently had to respond to questions such as, "What?" and "That is the first time I have ever heard of it."

In the course of providing practical guidance in response to the diverse questions of the countless foreign visitors to Japan, people working on the front lines of the hotel and tourism industries seem to be reminded every day of these distinctive interests and the uniqueness of Tokyo as a city.

Nobuko Suzuki, excerpt from 『Why Is Tokyo the World’s Number-One City?』, PHP Publishing.

default.p.n2dokkai-p63.vietnamese:
Person seeking advice:
I would like to ask for advice about a foreign colleague at my company. His Japanese is good and he does his job well, but as soon as 5:00 p.m., when the workday ends, he leaves immediately. My company is small, and because we are short-staffed, we frequently work overtime to help departments that have not finished their work. Of course, we are paid for the overtime. I cannot understand how my colleague can see people struggling and still leave without helping them.

Respondent A:
There is nothing wrong with leaving the company at 5:00 p.m. If you have finished your own work, you can go home. It may be considered un-Japanese in terms of work style, but I think this foreign employee is doing the right thing. If everyone works overtime every day, they will become exhausted and may very well suffer health problems. Shouldn't we see this as an opportunity to reconsider the Japanese style of working?

Respondent B:
I wonder what kind of employment contract this foreign employee signed with the company. If it states, "Working hours are until 5:00 p.m.; no overtime," then there is absolutely no problem. However, if it states, "The employee will work overtime when work is busy," then he is failing to comply with the contract. In any case, there is no reason for you to worry about it. This is an issue for the supervisor or company director to consider and resolve.

default.p.n2dokkai-p64.vietnamese:
Why does forgetting occur? In psychology, various theories have been proposed. The view that a memory gradually weakens over time, even though it was once remembered, is called the decay theory. This seems quite reasonable from an empirical standpoint, but is the passage of time really the only cause?

According to interference theory, remembering other things is what causes forgetting. In reality, when we learn many new things later, they become confused with and cause us to forget what we learned earlier. The idea that people are less likely to forget during sleep can also be explained by interference theory.

The retrieval failure theory is the hypothesis that experiences remain stored in the mind, but people fail to recall them. (Middle section omitted) No matter how much we remember, it is meaningless if we cannot retrieve it. Therefore, it is important to organize the material or prepare a variety of memory cues so that it will be easier to recall later.

From a different perspective, there is a hypothesis called repression theory. This theory holds that people repress unpleasant things deep in the unconscious so that they do not rise into conscious awareness. This is the way of thinking associated with the psychoanalytic school of Freud. (Later section omitted)

(Shin'ichi Ichikawa, "The Book That Changed the Way We Study," Iwanami Junior Shinsho)

default.p.n2dokkai-p68-g0.vietnamese:
The practice of collecting money from many people for a particular purpose has existed since ancient times, but recently crowdfunding over the Internet has become very popular. A person who wants to raise funds posts the purpose and significance of the project, along with the target amount and fundraising deadline, on the website of a crowdfunding service provider. People who view the information and wish to support it pay by credit card or similar methods. In many cases, projects accept contributions as small as 500 or 1,000 yen.

In the past, there was also the case of Professor Shinya Yamanaka, a Nobel Prize winner, who raised as much as 20 million yen when he sought 4 million yen for research expenses. In addition, nonprofit organizations (NPOs) and local governments sometimes use this method to raise funds to support victims of natural disasters or to fund traditional local festivals.

default.p.n2dokkai-p69-g0.vietnamese:
When two or more people come together with a common purpose, an organization is needed. Communication and teamwork are essential for operating an organization and enabling it to function effectively.

In an organization, positions arise in accordance with duties and responsibilities, and titles exist to indicate those positions. Depending on the company, titles may vary, such as representative, director, board member, department manager, team leader, supervisor, and so on.

Usually, we attach a person's position to their name when addressing them, don't we? We use forms such as Director XX, Department Manager XX, and Team Leader XX as a matter of course.

However, addressing someone by their position can sometimes unintentionally create a wall between us and the other person. Because of this, have you ever felt intimidated or hesitant and been unable to say what you wanted to say? Haven't many people nodded in agreement, thinking, “Yes, yes,” because they have experienced the same thing?

(Akira Yoshinaka, “Why Women Go to Disneyland Repeatedly,” Chukei Publishing)

default.p.n2dokkai-p72-g0.vietnamese:
Recently, food waste—the disposal and waste of food that is still edible—has become a serious concern. Japan's food waste in 2016 amounted to 6.43 million tons, and the government enacted a new law to reduce this amount. The largest sources of waste are food manufacturers, the food-service industry, and retailers such as supermarkets and convenience stores. As a result, more manufacturers are donating food that is still edible to food banks instead of throwing it away. Food banks distribute this food to places where it is needed. Some convenience stores also give customers reward points when they buy food that is close to its expiration date.

However, in reality, nearly half of all food waste comes from households. Consumers like us should also be careful not to waste the food ingredients we have bought. In addition, when buying fruits and vegetables, perhaps we should stop being overly concerned with their appearance.

default.p.n2dokkai-p73-g0.vietnamese:
In an experiment in which elephants had a mark shaped like an X placed on their faces and were shown a mirror, scientists observed them touching the mark with their trunks. A research team from Emory University in the U.S. state of Georgia and other organizations announced these findings in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The elephants appear to have the ability to recognize that the reflection in the mirror is themselves, not another elephant.

The experiment was conducted on three female Asian elephants kept at a zoo in New York City. When a white X was placed on their faces, researchers observed a 34-year-old elephant named “Happy” repeatedly touching the mark on her face in front of a mirror hung on the wall of her enclosure.

As a control, the researchers also drew an invisible X on the elephants’ faces using transparent paint, but Happy did not touch the mark at all. However, the same behavior was not observed in the other two elephants.

Until now, mirror experiments had led researchers to believe that self-recognition existed only in humans, apes, and dolphins. The researchers concluded that the evolution of self-recognition may be related to the complex social nature of animals.

default.p.n2dokkai-p74-g0.vietnamese:
What is communication? Put briefly and clearly, it is the act of exchanging meaning and feelings with one another. If information simply flows in one direction, it is not called communication. Surely, no one would call [ 1 ] communication. It is precisely because communication involves mutual interaction that it can be called communication.

What is mainly exchanged is meaning and feelings. Simply conveying information is not necessarily the same as communication. Communication does not only convey information; sharing and conveying feelings with one another is also an important role of communication. Whenever an incident or problem occurs, people often say, "We should have communicated properly beforehand." On one hand, this means that they should have explained the situation carefully and established more shared understanding of the underlying issues in advance. On the other hand, it means that they should not merely have exchanged information, but should also have increased emotional understanding and built, through communication, a trusting relationship strong enough to be repaired even if some misunderstanding or disagreement occurred.

Takashi Saito, 『Communication Skills』, Iwanami Shinsho

default.p.n2dokkai-p75-g0.vietnamese:
Have you ever folded origami? With the art of origami, a single sheet of paper can be turned into many things, such as birds—including cranes—animals, flowers, and boxes. Once completed, an origami piece is a three-dimensional object, but when unfolded, its original form is just one flat sheet of paper.

Are you thinking that origami is merely a children’s game? In fact, origami techniques have recently been applied to space engineering. Try imagining an artificial satellite. An artificial satellite flies using electricity from solar cells. Around the satellite is a large, thin, disk-shaped component: the solar panels. Origami techniques have been applied to these panels. First, the satellite panels are designed so that they can be folded like origami, and then they are folded into a compact shape. After being taken into space, they simply need to be unfolded and expanded. Research of this kind, particularly in the United States, is considered so important that it receives government funding.

In addition, the structure of ladybug wings is said to provide useful inspiration when manufacturing solar panels for artificial satellites. Like origami, ladybug wings are normally folded into a compact shape, but when the insect flies, they unfold into a three-dimensional form.

Ideas for inventions may be hidden in familiar things around us, such as origami and ladybugs.

default.p.n2dokkai-p76-g0.vietnamese:
There are many delicious foods around us, from cakes, custard pudding, whipped cream, and yogurt to pasta and bread. What these foods have in common is that they all use dairy products. Dairy products are widely used in our diets today. Try opening your refrigerator. You are sure to find some kind of dairy product inside. Dairy products make food taste milder and more harmonious, and they add richness and color to culinary culture. However, this kind of life, surrounded by dairy products, has only appeared relatively recently in the history of Japan.

Over the course of many years, a wide variety of dairy products have developed around the world. Butter and cheese, which we commonly use every day, developed under the influence of European and American countries. These European- and American-style dairy products account for only a very small part of the vast variety of dairy products found around the world. For example, nomadic people in Mongolia make alcohol from milk. Herders in Syria produce an unripened cheese that is dried until it becomes so hard that it is almost impossible to bite through. In India, people pour mildly sour yogurt over curry and eat it.

Masahiro Hirata, “10,000 Years of Humans and Milk,” Iwanami Junior Shinsho Library.

default.p.n2dokkai-p78-g0.vietnamese:
When we travel abroad and arrive at an airport, somehow we can sense the atmosphere of that country and society. I had always wondered why, but at one point I realized that it was because of the facial expressions of the people at that airport.

If everyone there has an expression suggesting that they are wary of others, we feel a harsh, oppressive atmosphere. Then a sense of tension—that this country is dangerous—runs through our entire body.

Conversely, when we encounter bright smiles, we develop a sense of reassurance that this is a warm and welcoming country. We naturally acquire a cheerful expression ourselves.

If possible, I hope Japan will be the latter kind of country. Until now, Japanese people have tended to underestimate the importance of facial expressions to some extent. If this changed so that, upon arriving at places such as Narita Airport, every Japanese person wore a cheerful expression, foreigners would feel reassured, and Japan’s image in the international community would certainly change significantly.

To spread such cheerful expressions, the most important thing is for each of us to wear one ourselves. Good and bad expressions both spread from person to person. If we wear cheerful expressions, our families, workplaces, entire neighborhoods, and society as a whole will also become more cheerful. Moreover, if all of Japan wore joyful expressions and this spread throughout the world, nothing could be more exciting or happier.

(According to Hiroshi Harashima and Hisao Baba, "What Has Changed Human Faces," Kawade Shobo Shinsha)

default.p.n2dokkai-p79-g1.vietnamese:
Eight months have passed since I began writing this little book. I have lost count of how many times I have wanted to give up halfway through.

I have plenty of material to write about. I have also prepared all the reference materials. However, whenever I begin writing, I clearly realize that my words seem dead—lifeless and lacking vitality. I have thought a great deal about why this happens. Then I suddenly realized the truth: there was no one to talk to.

I have a habit of telling whoever I happen to meet next about what I have read in books or what has just occurred to me. During a conversation, my thoughts continue to pour out depending on the other person’s reaction. Whether they are family members or colleagues at the university, whenever I catch them, they have to listen to me endlessly talk about what I am thinking until they are fed up. When I write a book, I receive none of this feedback.

Takao Suzuki, excerpt from "Language and Culture," Iwanami Shinsho.

① Moreover, mayonnaise has a very strong antibacterial effect. There are even experimental reports showing that when mayonnaise was applied to a certain disease-causing bacterium, the bacteria were killed within just a few dozen hours.

② Some people apparently think that anything can be safely stored in the refrigerator simply by putting it there—whether furikake*, salt, or soy sauce—but in fact, there are also things that should not be kept in the refrigerator.

③ For that reason, mayonnaise is best stored in a place out of direct sunlight. In summer, if you put it in the refrigerator, I recommend methods such as sealing it in a bag to prevent it from becoming too cold.

④ Mayonnaise is one of those things. Mayonnaise is made by emulsifying egg yolk with vinegar, salt, and vegetable oil. The emulsion is most stable at room temperatures of about 10 to 30°C; if the temperature is higher or lower, it becomes unstable and is likely to separate. When it separates, the oil, vinegar, and egg separate from one another, preventing the vinegar’s antibacterial effect from spreading evenly throughout the sauce. At the same time, the oil oxidizes, causing the sauce to spoil more quickly.

Edited by Hitoshi Takeuchi, from “Easy-to-Understand Useful Knowledge for the Brain,” Mikasa Shobo.

default.p.n2dokkai-p81-g0.vietnamese:
On March 11, 2011, there were about ten crows near the museum, but before the shaking caused by the earthquake began, they were not making any unusually loud noise. However, when the shaking started, they began making a commotion. When the shaking temporarily subsided※1, they returned to the branches, but whenever an aftershock occurred, they became noisy again. At least the crows I observed did not cry loudly because they had predicted the earthquake; they began making noise only after the earthquake vibrations reached the area. Tree branches shake in the wind anyway, so this is somewhat strange, but perhaps the branches swaying without any wind made the crows uncomfortable. Of course, it is also possible that they sensed sounds occurring simultaneously with the vibrations and then began to cry loudly.

There are many phenomena in animals that are said to precede earthquakes※2, but the problem is that it is very difficult to quantify※3 how loudly crows normally call. In addition, the way they make noise naturally differs from day to day. Therefore, even if someone says, “Come to think of it, they seemed noisier than usual that day!”, it is very difficult to make an accurate judgment.

Hajime Matsubara, “A Crow Textbook,” Raichosha Publishing.

default.p.n2dokkai-p82-g0.vietnamese:
Does eating breakfast improve academic performance?

(Section omitted) Thus, a scientific attitude means viewing things and phenomena with skepticism and questions. Abstracting observed things and phenomena to formulate a hypothesis is the first step in the process known as science.

However, when formulating a hypothesis, we often make one particular mistake. We confuse correlation with causation. Correlation is a relationship in which two events are simply associated with each other, whereas causation is a relationship in which two events are connected as cause and effect.

In 2003, the National Institute for Educational Policy published research showing that children who ate a full breakfast every day achieved good academic results. How did they know this?

Every year, the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology administers a nationwide academic achievement test and conducts a questionnaire survey at the same time. When the test results were compared with the questionnaire responses, it was found that most children with good results ate a full breakfast every day. Based on this result, some people began asserting, “If children eat breakfast, their academic performance will improve.”

Akira Ikegami, *An Introduction to Science*, NHK Publishing

When I was young (about 40 to 50 years ago), all boys and girls were fascinated by science. Dr. Ochanomizu and Dr. Shikishima, who had just appeared above, were both heroes of that era. Science, in other words, was a “dream of the future.” We were shown countless brilliant “pictures” of how the future would surely become a wonderful world. It really was such an age.

Half a century has passed since then. If we ask what happened to that “brilliant future,” flying cars over major cities and space travel for ordinary people have still not become reality, but computers, mobile phones, and car navigation systems have become completely widespread and familiar. One could even say that science has penetrated our lives more deeply than we imagined. Although it is still difficult to say that everyone around the world is enjoying its benefits, if we look at the overall average, isn’t everything progressing rather well?

Although young people today were born into that very “brilliant future,” few of them seem to become “science boys” or “science girls.” Moreover, they have no desire to become such people. If anything, they tend to prefer nature, love the natural world, and long for a slower lifestyle. One might even think that, compared with our generation, they are “moving backward scientifically.”

Hiroshi Mori, 『What Does Science Mean?』, Gentosha

Japan has an extremely rare custom, even by global standards. In many families, each member has their own dishes and chopsticks. Father’s bowl and chopsticks, mother’s bowl and chopsticks, little Taro’s, little Hanako’s—each family member has eating utensils intended specifically for them. This custom is reportedly called “Meimei-bashi” (“individual chopsticks”).

Many people are surprised to learn that this custom is exceptionally rare, no matter how wide the world is. In most countries, eating utensils differ only in quality, such as luxury or inexpensive items, or are divided according to use, such as everyday, ceremonial, or party tableware. It is virtually unheard of for each family member to own a separate set of eating utensils for personal use.

Masayuki Nishie, “An Extracurricular Lesson on Food,” Heibonsha.

default.p.n2dokkai-p86-g0.vietnamese:
Although it was not that long ago, discussions of food in society once focused almost exclusively on nutrition and how high in calories something was. Factors such as a dish's appearance and flavor, or the atmosphere of a restaurant, were rarely mentioned in the mass media. At that time, people were mainly interested in such issues as how to achieve the best possible growth for young children and maintain the health of adults.

Then came what was called the "age of plentiful food," and society changed completely. What should people eat to lose weight? Topics like this began to be repeated constantly on television and in magazines, and society accepted them without hesitation. Moreover, going somewhere to eat delicious food became a trend, and it could be said that people increasingly tended to rely on advertisements and trends, rather than their own sense of taste, when looking for something to eat.

Masayuki Nishie, from "An Extracurricular Lesson on Eating," Heibonsha.

default.p.n2dokkai-p88-g0.vietnamese:
Science begins with skepticism. First, let us try questioning things that are commonly accepted as facts. People generally say that the Earth is warming. But is that really true? Is global warming actually occurring?

In fact, there have also been scientists who were skeptical about global warming.

Looking at Earth’s history, the entire planet has repeatedly alternated between cold periods covered by glaciers and warm periods. If we consider this cycle, perhaps the Earth will not continue warming forever this time either, but will certainly enter another cold period eventually. This is the skeptical view of global warming.

Experts have responded to this view by arguing that the probability of an ice age arriving in the near future is extremely low, so this cannot be considered a particularly convincing argument.

Akira Ikegami, “An Introduction to Science,” NHK Publishing

The other day, when I visited a country in Central Asia, I was surprised to see that most of the people I met there carried mobile phones. I wondered whether the mobile-phone ownership rate there might actually be higher than in a “developed country” such as Japan. According to a friend from that country, there may be more people who own mobile phones than people who have telephones at home. My friend even told me that there is a joke that when nomads gather their sheep, they contact the sheep by mobile phone.

I see—the reason is probably that mobile phones are simpler and more convenient for both buyers and sellers than landlines. In Japan, it took a long time for landlines to become widespread. Countless public telephone booths were installed, and only afterward did mobile phones appear. That was not the case in this country. I found it fascinating to realize so clearly that the development of civilization and the way society changes are completely different in each country.

default.p.n2dokkai-p90-g0.vietnamese:
When describing a large area or an enormous quantity, people often use the expression “several times the size of Tokyo Dome.” This seems to make things easier to visualize than using numbers. Put another way, however, it means that many people cannot grasp the scale through ordinary numbers. Area and volume are normally expressed in familiar units such as meters and kilometers, so if they are given numerically, we should certainly be able to visualize them easily. If we hear that something is one million square meters, we only need to imagine a square with sides of 1,000 meters—that is, 1 kilometer. We can surely also imagine which part of the neighborhood where we live extends from one point to another. Of course, this would be meaningless without an elementary-school-level understanding of mathematics that 1,000 × 1,000 equals one million.

Even when a size is expressed in terms of Tokyo Dome, it is perfectly normal not to know approximately how large Tokyo Dome is. (Putting its width aside, its volume must be especially difficult to understand.) If it is given as a number, we can at least calculate—or estimate—how many days 10,000 cubic meters of beer would last if converted into the amount of beer we personally drink. Nothing is as concrete and easy to grasp as numbers.

Numbers are the clearest indicator for communicating the level or extent of something. Yet many people reject numbers and only want to know “how people feel about that number.” When television reports on a burst water pipe, simply stating how many liters of water leaked would allow people to understand, but instead reporters interview people nearby and try to get them to describe how terrible it was. They even seem to think that conveying such “people’s impressions” is what constitutes “accurate information.” When I follow news media coverage, I feel that the proportion of information that is impressionistic and subjective is gradually increasing.

default.p.n2dokkai-p92-g0.outline.1.note: Analyzes labor and electricity costs and proposes keeping places open at night only where necessary, while closing facilities in residential areas from evening until morning.
default.p.n2dokkai-p92-g0.outline.2.label: Author B: recognizing the role of essential infrastructure and the value of people
default.p.n2dokkai-p92-g0.outline.2.note: Author B acknowledges the labor shortage but asserts that convenience stores are important social infrastructure for night-time drivers and for maintaining human connections.
default.p.n2dokkai-p92-g0.outline.3.label: Author B: proposing that stores remain open at night for public safety
default.p.n2dokkai-p92-g0.outline.3.note: Convenience stores make residential areas safer at night; author B proposes improving working conditions for elderly people and foreigners and closing stores only in places with few residents.
default.p.n2dokkai-p92-g0.vietnamese:
[Viewpoint A]
The other day, during a television interview, I was surprised to hear a woman in her sixties say that it would be very inconvenient if convenience stores did not stay open 24 hours, because elderly people sometimes suddenly become ill. If something is needed when one is sick or injured, it should be bought and stored in advance. Thinking that when this woman was young, supermarkets closed at 7 p.m. and convenience stores closed at 11 p.m., I could not help thinking about how frightening it is to become too accustomed to convenience.

There was once a commercial showing young people suddenly wanting something to eat in the middle of the night and going to a convenience store to buy it. But is it really necessary to keep stores open for people like that? The cost is not limited to labor. What about electricity bills, for example? Since customer demand varies by location, it may make sense for some stores to operate 24 hours a day, but neighborhood stores could surely close from around 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. Doing so could also reduce electricity consumption.

[Viewpoint B]
The 24-hour operation of convenience stores is becoming a difficult problem. The major reason it is difficult to keep them open around the clock appears to be a labor shortage. Perhaps this means that closing at midnight is unavoidable when it is difficult to secure staff.

However, have convenience stores not become a presence worthy of being called social infrastructure? If convenience stores along national highways stopped selling goods at night, truck drivers who support the transportation industry would certainly face difficulties. Having vending machines is not enough. What matters is having people—employees—stationed there. Even without talking to one another, I feel that there is a connection among people working late into the night.

Even in residential areas, when I return home alone late at night, seeing the lights of a convenience store reassures me. If everything around me were pitch-dark, it would surely be frightening. I think convenience stores also contribute to public safety in Japan. Surely we could create a working environment that is convenient for both older people and foreign workers and somehow maintain sufficient staffing. I hope that nighttime closures will be limited to areas with few people at night.

default.p.n2dokkai-p94-g0.vietnamese:
The content of psychologist Endel Tulving's experiment was extremely simple: participants were asked to observe a room in which furniture, a desk, a coffee table, a TV, a computer, and other items had been placed in a disorderly arrangement.

After showing them the entire room, the researchers divided the participants into two groups and asked them questions. The first group was told, "Recall the items that were in the 'living room' just now," while the other was told, "Recall the items that were in the 'study.'"

What were the results? The group told that it was a "living room" remembered highly typical items such as a sofa and a TV, while the group told that it was a "study" remembered only things typical of a study, such as a computer, a desk, and piles of documents.

Some exceptional participants even insisted that there was "absolutely no computer" or that "there was a dictionary"—confidently claiming that something that was actually there was not, or that something that was not there was present.
